newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech cbank faces uphill battle with intervention.
newsitem.headline: Czech cbank faces uphill battle with intervention.

text.p: The Czech central bank (CNB), intervened on Friday for the second consecutive day to shore up the ailing crown, but dealers said the CNB faced an uphill battle if it was going to firm up market sentiment.

"The central bank is going to have a tough time keeping the crown up, sentiment is very weak. We may see London and New York wait until central bank activity eases and at about 1300 GMT they may jump on the crown," said Petr Korous of CSOB (Ceskoslodenska Obchodni Banka), the largest domestic foreign exchange player.

"The investment funds I think can sense what is happening -- the CNB is on the defensive and they (the funds) have more power than the central bank. They are playing a very dangerous game today," he added.

After warning the market for months it would not allow the crown to fall too much, the central bank first stepped into the market on Thursday with several rounds of intervention and vowed to continue buying crowns if necessary.

The CNB on Friday followed through with its promise, entering the market at about 0800 GMT by first checking rates and then striking deals at around four percent on the depreciation side of its dollar/mark parity. The bank also raised its one-week repo rate by 50 basis points to 12.90 percent.
Central bank officials were not immediately available to confirm the amounts of deals, but traders estimated the volumes to be smaller, at about 10 million marks at a time.
At the end of March, the CNB's foreign exchange reserves were almost unchanged from the month before at $11.7 billion.
The crown opened Friday at about 3.8 percent on the depreciation side of its dollar/mark basket midpoint, but lost ground to around -3.95 percent despite the repo rate rise.
Dealers said they thought the move was far too little to provide any real support for the crown.

"I don't think such a change in rates will effect the market at all. If the central bank is going to protect the crown it has to do something more significant, not just a few basis points," said Breta Tichanek of ING bank.
Added another trader: "The repo rate rise was already built into the market, so its effect is minimal."
Late on Thursday the CNB said it had decided to raise its repo rate, but had not set a target for how much it would rise instead allowing "market conditions" to be the determining factor.
Tomas Becvar of Komercni Banka said that while the CNB intervened at around five percent on the depreciation side of basket parity on Thursday, its Friday activities began at a higher level.
"They (the CNB) will try to keep it (the crown) under four percent, but so far it's been a fifty-fifty fight, I would say," Becvar added.

In explaining why it entered the market, the CNB said the crown's fall was due to fluctuations of several foreign currencies. It did not elaborate, but some traders said foreign investors were getting nervous over some emerging market economies troubled by a weak external position, such as Thailand.
